findings.title: Rogue ScreenConnect Installations Across Unrelated Hosts Suggest Worm-Like Activity
findings.summary_md: Huntress reported rogue ScreenConnect client installations appearing across unrelated hosts, with a modified ScreenConnect client propagating a four-stage VBScript chain to newly connected systems. The activity was observed in three incidents in August 2026 using varied initial-access lures, and the modified client re-sent the stager files to each new Host session, creating worm-like propagation over ScreenConnect connections. Huntress recommended reimaging affected hosts and warned that any sign of Windows Script Host or PowerShell execution in ScreenConnect server audit logs should raise suspicion.

findings.title: Rogue ScreenConnect Clients Spread Four-Stage VBScript Chain to Newly Connected Hosts
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News covered Huntress findings that three unrelated incidents used diverse initial access methods to trigger a four-stage VBScript chain leading to rogue ScreenConnect installations. The modified client propagated the stager scripts to server-side Host systems over new ScreenConnect connections, with incidents observed in August 2026. ConnectWise issued an advisory about file-transfer behavior in ScreenConnect sessions in response, recommending that customers disable technician file transfer until a fix was available.

findings.title: ScreenConnect security advisory: Precautionary extension disabling and partner guidance
findings.summary_md: ConnectWise published a security advisory reporting unauthorized access to ScreenConnect partner accounts and deployment of unauthorized remote-access software in customer environments. As a precaution, it disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across approximately 400 partner environments and told on-premises customers to disable them manually. The advisory recommended reviewing authentication logs, extension installation records, administrative activity, Run Command history, and Toolbox records, and warned that disabling extensions does not remove already-established malicious software or persistence.
